summary: Describes how a restarting OSPF router can signal its neighbors that it is restarting, so they do not drop it and routing keeps working. Hello packets would otherwise cause neighbors to forget the router. This memo is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: When a router reboots, it has forgotten which neighbours it was talking to. The Hello packets it sends do not mention them, so they assume the link is gone and drop the adjacency. RFC 4812 adds one bit to the Hello packet that says the router is restarting and that missing neighbours should be ignored for now.

questions: how does ospf graceful restart work
what is the ospf rs bit
how does ospf avoid resetting adjacencies on restart
subtitle: A flag in the OSPF Hello packet that tells neighbours to hold on to an adjacency while a router is restarting.

tldr.problem: A router that restarts its OSPF software comes back not knowing which neighbours it had, so its Hello packets omit them and those neighbours tear the adjacencies down.
tldr.mechanism: The restarting router sets a new RS bit in the Extended Options TLV of the Link-Local Signaling block in its Hello packets, and neighbours that understand it skip the two-way connectivity check until the router has resynchronised its link state database.
tldr.outcome: It only works where the neighbours support it; the rest simply reset the adjacency. The RFC records a vendor-specific mechanism that predates the standardised Graceful OSPF Restart, and says it is not an IETF standard.

facts.label: Carries the RS bit
facts.value: Extended Options TLV of the Link-Local Signaling block

facts.label: Hello packets that must not set it

today: RFC 4812 is an Informational document from March 2007 and has not been obsoleted or updated. The RFC states that it records a vendor-specific mechanism, that it needs support from the neighbouring routers to work, and that it is not an IETF standard, and it notes that it predates the standardised Graceful OSPF Restart in RFC 3623.

sections.title: The Problem With a Router That Forgets Its Neighbours
sections.content:
OSPF is a link-state intra-domain routing protocol used in IP networks. Routers find new neighbours and detect unreachable ones with the Hello subprotocol, and Hello packets are also used to confirm two-way connectivity within a period of time.

While performing a graceful restart of its OSPF software, a router needs to stop its neighbours from resetting their adjacencies. After a reload, though, a router may not know which neighbours it had adjacencies with in its previous incarnations. If such a router sends a Hello packet on an interface and that packet does not list some neighbours, those neighbours will reset the adjacency with the restarting router.

The technique in this document lets a restarting router tell its neighbours that it may not know about some of them yet, and that the absence of some router IDs in the Hello packets should be ignored.

The abstract is explicit about the status of this mechanism. It describes a vendor-specific mechanism, notes that it requires support from the neighbouring routers, records that it was proposed before Graceful OSPF Restart came into existence, and says it is implemented and supported by at least one major vendor and is deployed in the field. Its purpose is to capture the details of the mechanism for public use, and it is not an IETF standard.
sections.plainLanguage: OSPF neighbours check each other's Hello packets to confirm the link is working both ways. A router that has just rebooted cannot list the neighbours it had before, so its neighbours think it has gone and drop the link.

sections.title: The RS Bit in the Extended Options TLV
sections.content:
With the restart signalling solution, a new bit called RS, for restart signal, is introduced into the Extended Options TLV in the Link-Local Signaling block defined in RFC 4813. The value of this bit is 0x00000002. It sits next to the LR bit, which is defined in RFC 4811, and the remaining positions of the TLV are shown as unused in the figure the RFC gives.

A router should set the RS bit in the Extended Options TLV attached to a Hello packet when it is not known that all neighbours are listed in that packet, but the restarting router wants them to preserve their adjacencies. The RS bit must not be set in Hello packets longer than RouterDeadInterval seconds, so that the signal cannot be used to hold an adjacency open indefinitely.

The bit is carried inside the existing Link-Local Signaling block, which is the mechanism RFC 4813 defines for carrying information about the local link in OSPF packets. The IANA considerations of this document point to the IANA considerations section of RFC 4813 for the definitions of the Extended Options bits.
sections.plainLanguage: The signal is a single bit carried in a block that OSPF already has, next to another bit of the same kind. It tells the neighbour that the list of neighbours in this Hello packet may be incomplete.

sections.title: How a Neighbour Handles a Restart Signal
sections.content:
When a router receives a Hello packet containing the Link-Local Signaling block with the Extended Options TLV that has the RS bit set, it should skip the two-way connectivity check with the announcing neighbour. That means it should not generate a 1-WayReceived event for the neighbour if it does not find its own router ID in the list of neighbours, provided that the neighbour's finite state machine for that neighbour is in the Full state.

The router should also send a unicast Hello back to the sender in reply to a Hello packet with the RS bit set, which speeds up the learning of previously known neighbours. When sending such a reply, care must be taken to ensure that the RS bit is clear in it, so the reply does not itself look like another restart.

Two additional fields are introduced in the neighbour data structure. The RestartState flag indicates that a Hello packet with the RS bit set has been received and that the local router expects its neighbour to go through the link state database resynchronisation procedure defined in RFC 4811. The ResyncTimeout timer is a single-shot timer limiting the delay between the first Hello packet with the RS bit set and the start of that resynchronisation, and its length is RouterDeadInterval seconds.

When a Hello packet with the RS bit set is received and the RestartState flag is not already set for that neighbour, the router sets the flag and starts the ResyncTimeout timer. If the timer expires, the flag is cleared and a 1-WayReceived event is generated for the neighbour, which resets the adjacency in the ordinary way. If the neighbour starts the link state database resynchronisation procedure while the timer is running, the timer is cancelled, and the flag is also cleared when the resynchronisation completes.

Two or more routers on the same segment cannot have Hello packets with the RS bit set at the same time, as can be the case when two or more routers restart at about the same time. In that situation the routers should clear the RestartState flag, cancel the ResyncTimeout timer, and generate a 1-WayReceived event.
sections.plainLanguage: The neighbour ignores the missing names in the Hello packet, but only for a limited time. If the restarting router does not catch up before the timer expires, the neighbour drops the adjacency as it normally would.

sections.title: Ensuring Topology Stability
sections.content:
Under certain circumstances it may be desirable to stop announcing the restarting router as fully adjacent, if continuing to do so could lead to routing loops. To provide that, a configurable option is available on the neighbouring routers that instructs the OSPF process to follow a particular set of rules.

When a router schedules a routing table calculation because of a change in the contents of its link state database, it should also reset all adjacencies with restarting routers, that is, with the routers whose RestartState flag is set. It does this by clearing the RestartState neighbour flags, cancelling any running ResyncTimeout timers, and generating the 1-WayReceived events for the neighbour state machines.
sections.plainLanguage: If the network changes while a router is restarting, its neighbours can be told to stop treating it as fully connected. That avoids a routing loop, at the cost of the restart being abandoned early.

sections.title: Compatibility and Security
sections.content:
The technique requires cooperation from the neighbouring routers. If the neighbours do not support it, they will simply reset the adjacency, which is the behaviour without the mechanism.

The security considerations section is short and says that the described technique does not introduce any new security issues into the OSPF protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: The mechanism only helps where the neighbouring routers also understand it. Where they do not, the adjacency is reset as before, and the RFC adds no new security issues of its own.

items.text: OSPF routers find new neighbours and detect unreachable ones with the Hello subprotocol, and Hello packets confirm two-way connectivity within a period of time.

items.title: The restart problem
